NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Moderate concern: Data were collected in two rounds (August and December 2022) with a planned sample of 630 households assuming a 10% non-response rate (PDF Page 4, Table 1), but the paper never reports actual household response rates, achieved sample sizes in either round, or between-round attrition. Table 2 also omits microbial quality data for Babile without explanation (PDF Page 6).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable / Uncontrolled descriptive design: The study is purely descriptive and makes no causal effect estimates; the authors explicitly note that no statistical associations between coliform levels and sanitary risks were explored, and no multivariable adjustment for town- or household-level confounders was conducted (PDF Pages 5-6).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / Descriptive institutional operationalization: National governance mandates (2013 MoWIE National Guidelines for Urban Water Supply and Sewerage Services; One WASH National Programme / One WASH PLUS) and local utility/Water Board structures are accurately referenced as benchmarks (PDF Pages 2-3, 8-10), and institutional support/governance indicators are structured via the How tough is WASH framework (Table 3), but legal/regulatory compliance is assessed primarily through unverified key-informant interviews rather than documentary audits of municipal bylaws, utility charters, financial ledgers, or regulatory records.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Physical and water-quality measurements used recognized tools—WHO sanitary inspection checklists, membrane filtration for microbial CFU/100 mL, Palintest DPD visual color comparator for free residual chlorine, and ArcGIS Digital Elevation Modeling for flood risk (PDF Pages 4-5). However, water quality relied on limited point-in-time grab samples with no historical utility records available (PDF Page 6), household tariff payment and climate exposure relied on self-report (diverging from manager accounts, PDF Page 7), and qualitative findings lacked direct quotes or inter-coder reliability reporting.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Water supply resilience outcomes combined objective physical/microbial tests (CFU/100 mL at source, DPD free residual chlorine, WHO sanitary inspection, DEM flood vulnerability in Table 2) with subjective household and key-informant perceptions. However, quantitative household survey outcomes are reported only as sparse prose fragments without denominators, confidence intervals, or round-by-round breakdowns (PDF Pages 5-8), and Table 2 omits Babile's microbial count.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern (selective/incomplete descriptive reporting): Although 630 households were sampled across 10 towns and two seasonal rounds (August and December 2022; PDF Pages 3-4), no socio-demographic table, response rate, town-level survey table, or seasonal comparison between August and December rounds is reported; only isolated summary percentages appear in prose (PDF Pages 7-8). Similarly, qualitative results include zero verbatim participant quotations, and no pre-registered protocol or analysis plan is cited.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Study towns (n=10) were purposively selected from two climate-vulnerable zones in Oromia and Somali regions (PDF Page 4). Within towns, simple random sampling of households was restricted to utility customer lists of households already using piped water (PDF Page 4), systematically excluding unserved/unpiped town residents—up to 80% of households in towns such as Aweday where piped coverage was only 20% (PDF Pages 2-3).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The study clearly states its objectives at the end of the Introduction: to identify current and potential risks to small-town water utilities from climate stresses using the How tough is WASH conceptual framework and to adapt/propose monitoring indicators for town water utilities in Eastern Ethiopia.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Introduction, final paragraph (PDF Page 2)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collected across 10 small-town utilities—combining household surveys, WHO sanitary inspections, microbial and free residual chlorine water tests, ArcGIS/DEM flood-risk mapping, and semi-structured interviews with utility technicians, managers, and Water Board community representatives—directly map onto the six domains of the How tough is WASH framework to address the stated objectives.
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods: Study approach & Method of data collection (PDF Pages 3-5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative descriptive/framework approach using semi-structured key-informant interviews with utility technicians, utility managers, and Water Board community representatives is appropriate for investigating institutional support, operational governance, maintenance bottlenecks, and local coping practices that cannot be captured by infrastructure inspection alone.
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods: Study approach & Method of data collection (PDF Pages 4-5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Semi-structured interview topic guides were developed from the How tough is WASH framework (S2 Appendix), translated into local languages (Oromiffa/Oromia and Somali), conducted in local languages with all utility operators and managers plus one community board representative per town across the 10 towns, audio-recorded, transcribed, and translated into English.
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods: Study approach & Method of data collection (PDF Pages 4-5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors state that transcripts were coded deductively using a predefined list of codes based on How tough is WASH indicators, but they provide no details on coder numbers, coding reconciliation, saturation, or how conflicting stakeholder accounts within a utility were resolved, nor do they show any coding matrix or primary excerpts.
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods: Data analysis (PDF Page 5); Results §§3-6 (PDF Pages 6-8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Although specific town-level operational observations are summarized in narrative prose (e.g., anecdotal groundwater decline in Fafen, 5-15 day monthly interruptions in Awaday, irregular Woreda/Zonal meetings), the Results section contains zero verbatim quotations or structured qualitative evidence tables from technicians, managers, or community representatives to substantiate the authors' interpretations, and researcher reflexivity is not discussed.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: There is clear conceptual alignment across the six-domain How tough is WASH interview guides, deductive framework coding, domain-by-domain presentation of institutional/operational findings, and the resulting adaptation of utility indicators in Table 3.
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods (PDF Pages 4-5); Results §§3-7 & Table 3 (PDF Pages 6-10)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.1: Is the sampling strategy relevant to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Sample size (n=630) was calculated using a single population proportion formula (50% resilience, 4% margin of error, 95% CI, 10% non-response), allocated proportionally across the 10 study towns (Table 1), with simple random sampling from each town water utility's list of piped-water households, alongside census assessment of all utility sources and reservoirs in the 10 towns.
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods: Study approach & Table 1 (PDF Pages 3-4)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.2: Is the sample representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: First, the 10 towns were purposively rather than probabilistically selected from two regions. Second, household sampling frames were restricted to utility customer lists of households already using piped water, excluding unpiped town residents (up to 80% of households in low-coverage towns like Aweday at 20% coverage). Third, achieved respondent demographics are never reported to verify representativeness.
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods: Study area & Study approach (PDF Pages 2-4); Results (PDF Pages 5-8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.3: Are the measurements appropriate?
domain_ratings.justification: Survey and observational instruments were grounded in the published How tough is WASH framework and WHO sanitary inspection forms, translated and back-translated into Oromiffa and Somali, digitized in Kobo Toolbox, and paired with membrane filtration microbial testing, Palintest DPD free residual chlorine measurement, and ArcGIS DEM flood modeling. (Single/two-round grab-sample limitations for water quality are acknowledged on PDF Page 6.)
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods: Method of data collection & Data analysis (PDF Pages 4-5); Results §1 (PDF Page 6)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.4: Is the risk of nonresponse bias low?
domain_ratings.justification: Although a 10% non-response allowance was built into the target sample size of 630 households across two data collection rounds (August and December 2022), the paper never reports how many households actually participated in either round, the achieved response rate, reasons for non-participation, or missingness (besides an unexplained blank cell for Babile's microbial count in Table 2).
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods: Study approach & Table 1 (PDF Pages 3-4); Results & Table 2 (PDF Pages 5-8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.5: Is the statistical analysis appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Descriptive analysis is appropriate in principle for a descriptive resilience assessment, but actual quantitative reporting is severely incomplete: no tabular household survey statistics, exact numerators/denominators, confidence intervals, town-by-town survey distributions, or comparisons between the August and December 2022 rounds are presented, leaving only isolated prose summaries (e.g., 'more than half', 'more than 70%', '9%').
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods: Data analysis (PDF Page 5); Results §§3-4 (PDF Pages 7-8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Operationalizing the six-domain How tough is WASH resilience framework for piped utilities inherently requires combining physical/microbial/GIS infrastructure assessments and representative household user data with qualitative accounts of management, staffing, supply chains, and intergovernmental support.
domain_ratings.where_found: Introduction (PDF Page 2); Materials and methods: Study approach & Method of data collection (PDF Pages 3-5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Quantitative household survey metrics, sanitary/microbial/chlorine measurements, DEM flood modeling, and qualitative interviews are integrated directly within each of the six thematic resilience domains in the Results section and jointly inform the revised utility-specific framework in Table 3.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: The integrated findings are coherently synthesized in the Discussion and Table 3 to show how higher-level institutional and staffing gaps cascade into inadequate water treatment/testing, unbilled/unmetered water use, emergency vulnerability, and household reliance on unimproved sources, justifying specific indicator additions for utility-managed piped systems.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly note and explain discrepancies across data streams—most notably contrasting household survey self-reports where over half claimed regular bill payment against utility manager interviews reporting inconsistent payment due to meter shortages, estimated billing, and meter vandalism, as well as contrasting self-reported household chlorination against low measured free residual chlorine.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results §3 Management and governance & §4 Community governance and engagement (PDF Page 7)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Neither empirical strand fully satisfies the reporting and methodological standards of its tradition: the qualitative component lacks verbatim participant quotes, coding verification details, and researcher reflexivity (especially noting that consent was obtained in front of a local water utility expert, PDF Page 5), while the quantitative component purposively selected towns, excluded non-piped town residents, omitted actual response rates across two survey rounds, and failed to report complete descriptive survey tables or denominators.
domain_ratings.where_found: Materials and methods (PDF Pages 3-5); Results (PDF Pages 5-8)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Geremew et al. (2024) conducted a convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional assessment of 10 small-town piped water utilities in Eastern Ethiopia (Oromia and Somali regions) across August and December 2022, applying and adapting the six-domain 'How tough is WASH' climate-resilience framework. Per MMAT (2018) guidance, no numeric composite score is calculated, and overall methodological quality is bounded by the weakest empirical components (Moderate-to-high methodological concern). Strengths include clear research objectives (S1, S2), multi-modal integration across WHO sanitary inspections, membrane-filtration microbial testing, DPD residual chlorine testing, ArcGIS DEM flood-risk mapping, household surveys, and semi-structured stakeholder interviews (5.1-5.3), and explicit reconciliation of divergences between household self-reports and utility manager interviews regarding bill payment and water treatment (5.4). However, substantial limitations affect both empirical strands (5.5 = No): towns were purposively sampled and household random sampling was restricted to utility piped-water customer lists—excluding up to 80% of residents in low-coverage towns like Aweday (4.2 = No); actual household response rates, achieved sample sizes across the two seasonal rounds, socio-demographic characteristics, and tabular survey denominators/confidence intervals are omitted (4.4 = Can't tell; 4.5 = Can't tell; plus an unexplained missing microbial value for Babile in Table 2); and qualitative findings are presented solely as narrative summaries without a single verbatim quotation, coding audit detail, or reflexivity regarding consenting participants in the presence of a local water utility expert (1.3 = Can't tell; 1.4 = No).
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (per MMAT 2018 narrative guidance, no numeric score; strong mixed-methods integration [5.1-5.4 Yes], but overall quality is constrained by weaknesses in qualitative substantiation [1.4 No; 1.3 Can't tell] and quantitative representativeness and reporting transparency [4.2 No; 4.4-4.5 Can't tell; 5.5 No])
raw_response.study_design_identified: Convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional study combining a descriptive household survey (target n=630 across two rounds), sanitary/microbial/chlorine water quality and GIS/DEM assessments, and semi-structured qualitative interviews with utility technicians, managers, and board community representatives across 10 small towns
raw_response.where_found_summary: Objectives & institutional background: Abstract (PDF Page 1), Introduction (PDF Pages 1-2), Management of town water utilities (PDF Page 3). Sampling, instruments, laboratory/GIS methods, analysis & ethics: Materials and methods (PDF Pages 2-5, Table 1). Empirical findings & modified framework: Results §§1-7 (PDF Pages 5-10, Tables 2-3). Synthesis & policy alignment: Discussion & Conclusion (PDF Pages 8-11).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study explicitly employs a primary mixed-methods cross-sectional design ('employing both quantitative and qualitative methods', PDF Page 3) that integrates quantitative descriptive data (household survey, WHO sanitary inspection scores, microbial/chlorine tests, DEM flood risk) with qualitative semi-structured interviews (utility technicians, managers, and Water Board community representatives) across six domains of the How tough is WASH framework, with no randomized or quasi-experimental comparator. Therefore, MMAT (with the Quantitative Descriptive 4.1-4.5 block alongside Qualitative 1.1-1.5 and Mixed Methods 5.1-5.5) is the exact matching appraisal tool.
